name: That's The One
tagline: Planning workspace for wedding and event planners: clients, vendors, timelines, budgets and checklists in one place.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Underneath the category language, vertical planning software is structured CRUD: events, clients, vendors, line-item budgets, a dated timeline, repeatable checklists and a read-only view you can hand to a couple. An agent can produce a working version of all of that in a weekend, and for a solo planner running two or three events at a time it will genuinely be enough. What does not come out of the box is the part clients see and feel: tidy mobile layout, printable schedules that do not look like a spreadsheet dump, and checklist templates that already know what happens twelve weeks out. You also inherit the boring jobs the SaaS was quietly doing, namely backups, hosting and the moment a vendor asks for a PDF at 11pm. Build it if you want your own schema; pay if the client-facing surface is part of what you are selling.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you create an event, attach clients and vendors, track a budget against actuals, work a dated checklist, and publish a read-only link clients can open.
requirements: Node and a local SQLite file
a host and a domain if clients need to open the shared link
an email API key if you want reminder emails, otherwise skip email entirely
your own checklist templates, typed in once
whatYouLose: Prebuilt timeline and checklist templates based on how events actually run
A client-facing surface that looks professional on a phone without you styling it
Contracts, invoices, payment schedules and anything resembling e-sign
Vendor directories, shared documents and real multi-user access for assistants
Someone else handling backups, uptime and the data migration when you change your mind about the schema
moatNotes: The defensible bit is not the database, it is the templates plus the client-facing polish. Both are slow to recreate and neither is technically hard.
whyPeopleStillPay: Planners are selling calm. A tool that already knows the standard twelve-month arc of an event, renders a clean schedule your clients can read on a phone, and never requires you to debug anything on a Friday night is worth a subscription, because the alternative is doing unpaid sysadmin work during your busiest season. The DIY build is fine for your own internal tracking and gets awkward the moment a paying client or a venue coordinator has to use it.
notes: Vertical SaaS for a service business: the software is easy, the opinionated defaults are the product.
prompt:
Build a local-first event planning workspace for a single professional planner.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js with the App Router, TypeScript, React Server Components where sensible
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, one file at ./data/app.db, schema created on first run
- Tailwind for styling, no component library
- Zod for form validation
- Runs with `npm run dev` on port 3000, no Docker, no external services

Data model:
- Event: name, type, date, venue, status, notes
- Contact: name, role (client or vendor), company, email, phone, linked to an event
- BudgetLine: event, category, description, estimated amount, actual amount, paid boolean
- TaskTemplate: name plus ordered items, each item with a label and an offset in days relative to the event date
- Task: event, label, due date, done boolean, assigned contact (optional)

Features that must work:
1. Event list and event detail page with tabs for Overview, Contacts, Budget, Timeline
2. Applying a TaskTemplate to an event generates Tasks with due dates computed from the event date
3. Budget tab shows estimated total, actual total, variance per category, and outstanding unpaid lines
4. Timeline tab is a date-sorted task list with inline done toggles and an overdue indicator
5. A read-only share page at /share/[token] per event, showing date, timeline and key contacts, no auth, token generated on demand and revocable
6. A print stylesheet so the share page and the timeline print to clean A4
7. CSV export of contacts, budget lines and tasks

Explicitly out of scope: user accounts, payments, invoicing, e-signature, file uploads, email sending, telemetry, analytics, any hosted API.

Seed the database with one example event and two task templates, a twelve-month wedding arc and a short corporate event arc. Keep any config in .env and commit a .env.example. Write a README with run steps and one paragraph on how to back up the SQLite file.
